title: When policy depends on data you don’t have: The operational gap between lab-dependent criteria and claims adjudication
summary: Electronic health records integrations with genetic testing increases operational efficiency, enhances the provider experience and offers precision medicine at scale.
body_markdown:
Health plans have long used clinical criteria to determine coverage. Prior authorization and medical policy are intended to help providers and patients use diagnostics (and therapies) appropriately based on diagnosis, disease severity, and clinical need.


However, applying these criteria has become more operationally complex as coverage policies increasingly rely on objective clinical data (lab values, biomarkers, and longitudinal measures) that are not included in the initial transaction itself.


In most models, health plans define coverage policy for therapies, while pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) operationalize those policies through automated adjudication systems. When a claim is submitted, the PBM evaluates it in real time against payer-defined rules using the data available within the transaction. If required clinical evidence is not available at that moment, the system cannot fully apply the policy and the workflow shifts to manual retrieval.


### This creates a structural challenge: the information required to apply policy is often not available at the point of adjudication.


Industry research reflects the operational impact of this gap. The American Medical Association reports that[94% of physicians say prior authorization delays access to necessary care](https://www.ama-assn.org/press-center/ama-press-releases/toll-prior-authorization-exceeds-alleged-benefits-say-physicians?) , while[80% report that patients have abandoned treatment due to prior authorization struggles](https://www.ama-assn.org/press-center/ama-press-releases/toll-prior-authorization-exceeds-alleged-benefits-say-physicians?) .


## A structural challenge across therapeutic areas


GLP-1 receptor agonists provide a clear example. Coverage policies often require confirmation of diabetes through HbA1c thresholds, along with evidence of prior therapy use and ongoing monitoring of response.[Clinical standards from the American Diabetes Association (ADA)](https://diabetesjournals.org/care/article/49/Supplement_1/S27/163926/2-Diagnosis-and-Classification-of-Diabetes?) position HbA1c as a central measure for both diagnosis and management. Yet HbA1c values are not transmitted with pharmacy claims. As a result, when a prescription is adjudicated, the PBM system cannot verify whether criteria are met. The claim is pended or rejected, and the plan must request laboratory documentation and review the case manually even if the patient ultimately will qualify.


Other chronic condition therapies follow the same structure. Treatments for cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, and diabetes frequently depend on lab thresholds such as LDL cholesterol, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), or HbA1c. Guidance from organizations such as the[American College of Cardiology](https://professional.heart.org/en/science-news/2026-guideline-on-the-management-of-dyslipidemia/top-things-to-know?) and[ADA](https://diabetesjournals.org/care/article/49/Supplement_1/S246/163914/11-Chronic-Kidney-Disease-and-Risk-Management?) relies on these measures to guide therapy use. Still, these data points remain external to the adjudication process used to apply coverage policy.


In autoimmune conditions, biologic treatments for diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or inflammatory bowel disease are often tied to evidence of active inflammation. Markers like C-reactive protein (CRP) or erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), referenced in guidance from the[American College of Rheumatology](https://rheumatology.org/api/asset/blt65fc8b2649e03455?) , are used to assess disease activity and treatment appropriateness. However, these values reside in laboratory systems and are not available within the adjudication workflow, requiring plans to retrieve them before applying policy.


A similar pattern appears in oncology. Many targeted therapies depend on molecular or genetic biomarkers (EGFR mutations, HER2 overexpression, or BRCA variants) to determine eligibility. The[National Cancer Institute](https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/types/biomarker-testing-cancer-treatment?) has emphasized the central role of biomarker testing in modern cancer treatment. Yet these results are typically stored in pathology or genomic lab systems, separate from the administrative systems used to adjudicate claims.


From an operational perspective, the outcome is consistent. When required clinical data is not available at the time a claim is adjudicated, the system cannot fully evaluate payer-defined rules. The workflow then shifts to manual provider outreach, documentation requests, chart review, and resubmission cycles.


In this model, the process depends on an initial rejection before the necessary evidence can be gathered and evaluated. As the complexity of therapies increases, particularly in specialty pharmacy, this approach is becoming more difficult to sustain.


## Why this is relevant now


Several converging trends make this gap more visible and more difficult to manage within existing workflows.


First, the rapid growth of higher-cost therapies, particularly specialty drugs and GLP-1s, has increased both the financial stakes and the need for precise coverage criteria. Plans are under greater pressure to ensure therapies are used in clinically appropriate populations, which often requires lab-based validation.


Second, coverage policies themselves have become more specific. Rather than relying on broad diagnosis categories, many policies now reference measurable thresholds to define eligibility. This increases reliance on data that is not included in claims transactions.


Finally, regulatory and market scrutiny around prior authorization has intensified. Payers are expected to reduce administrative burden while maintaining appropriate utilization controls. This makes workflows that depend heavily on manual documentation retrieval more difficult to justify and sustain.


Taken together, instead of changing what coverage policies require, these shifts are making it more challenging to apply those policies efficiently using traditional workflows.


## How Labcorp supports faster, more complete adjudication


Labcorp enables health plans and PBMs to incorporate laboratory data directly into adjudication workflows, helping ensure that the clinical evidence required to apply coverage policy is available when claims are processed.


By making objective diagnostic data accessible at the point of adjudication, Labcorp helps:


- **Reduce reliance on post-claim documentation requests**
- **Minimize manual prior authorization review for routine cases**
- **Support consistent application of coverage criteria**
- **Accelerate time to appropriate therapy**


As coverage policies continue to rely on lab based evidence, improving access to that data within adjudication systems can play a critical role in reducing administrative burden and supporting more efficient coverage operations.
